subtitle: Arguing in form, and the shape of an essay
words.intro: The German school essay is called an *Erörterung*. It has a thesis, an antithesis and a synthesis, and generations have been graded on it. Germans carry it with them. Ask one where to go for lunch, and you’ll get the arguments for, the arguments against and a conclusion.

grammar[0].fact: In a German argument, attacking the *argument* is polite, and is thought rather friendly. Disagreeing is no insult. It may surprise you at first, and then you’ll start to miss it. Attacking the person is a different matter, as *Sie sind ein Idiot* will get you sued: insult is a crime here.

grammar[1].blocks[2].text: The first half is the view the author *rejects*. The answer is in the sondern-half.
grammar[1].fact: German pupils learn to write essays in a pattern: strongest argument last on your own side, and weakest first on the other. It’s been taught for over a century. So if a German colleague leaves their best point until the very end, it’s not a slip. It’s school.

document.intro: A real page from a German handbook on writing letters. Here’s the question of this chapter, settled about 1900: it quotes a very long sentence and says it’s *keineswegs wirklich falsch*, but it should be avoided. Try the first long quotation. Dr. Brummer loves it.
document.fact: Its rule, at the end of the second paragraph, is one Frau Huber could sign: *Je weniger man derartige Zusammenziehungen … anwendet, um so besser ist es*. It took the author a hundred words to say it.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Answer each with a concession, then disagree.
reading.intro: You were promised this. The Hofstraße literary society has at last held the great debate: *Ist der lange Satz besser als der kurze?* For the long sentence: Dr. Brummer. For the short one: Frau Huber. Four minutes each. Maya has the bell.
reading.fact: German sentences really can save the verb for the end, and writers have used this for drama. Mark Twain joked that a German reader dives into a sentence and comes up on the other side of the Atlantic with the verb in his mouth.
